ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
An athlete with a mass $m = 70 \, \text{kg}$ slides freely down a slope from point A at a height $h = 10 \, \text{m}$ with an initial speed of $10 \, \text{m/s}$. All resistances are negligible, and the plane at point B is taken as the zero potential surface.

1. The kinetic energy $E_k$ of the athlete at point A; do not add any other content.
2. The mechanical energy of the athlete at point A is $E_A$.
3. The speed of the athlete when reaching point B is $v_B$. ($g = 10\text{m/s}^2$)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: An athlete with a mass $m = 70 \, \text{kg}$ slides freely down a slope from point A at a height $h = 10 \, \text{m}$ with an initial speed of $10 \, \text{m/s}$. All resistances are negligible, and the plane at point B is taken as the zero potential surface. 1. The kinetic energy $E_k$ of the athlete at point A; do not add any other content. 2. The mechanical energy of the athlete at point A is $E_A$. 3. The speed of the athlete when reaching point B is $v_B$. ($g = 10\text{m/s}^2$)
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, point A is marked at a relatively high position on the left side, and the track slides downward from A to the lowest point in the middle, where point B is marked; the horizontal line where B is located serves as the reference plane, and there is a vertical height difference h from A to this horizontal line. Reasoning: At point A, the athlete's mass m=70 kg, and the initial velocity v_A=10 m/s, so the kinetic energy E_k(A)=1/2*m*v_A^2=1/2*70*10^2=3500 J. Taking the B plane as the zero potential energy plane, the height of point A is h=10 m, so the gravitational potential energy at point A is U_A=mgh=70*10*10=7000 J. The mechanical energy at point A is E_A=E_k(A)+U_A=3500+7000=10500 J. Resistance can be ignored, and mechanical energy is conserved; when reaching point B, U_B=0, therefore 1/2*m*v_B^2=10500, obtaining v_B^2=300, v_B=10sqrt(3) m/s.
